## Purpose and scope

This file carries the mathematics behind the `dwlsmv` Stata command and the code that
verifies it. Design decisions, sparse-category policy, and open questions live in the
companion working document, not here.

**Evidence status.** Development validation, preregistered numerical studies, and internal
decision records supporting this derivation are maintained in the private development repository
and are not distributed with this release; that is the "companion working document" above. The
chunks below execute when the file is rendered, and are the derivation's own checks. Citations of
the form E-001 name one item of the private record; the specification's *Evidence status*
paragraph explains them.

Every numerical claim below is produced by a chunk in this file. Nothing is transcribed.

Scope for v1: ordinal and binary indicators only, no continuous indicators, no
covariates. Binary is the $K_j = 2$ special case of the general ordinal derivation
throughout, not a separate path. The staged construction follows Muthén (1984).

## Setup

### The bivariate normal CDF

The derivations need $\Phi_2(a,b;\rho)$ repeatedly. To keep this file dependency-free
and reproducible, it is defined here by its one-dimensional integral representation,

$$\Phi_2(a,b;\rho) = \int_{-\infty}^{a} \phi(x)\,
  \Phi\!\left(\frac{b-\rho x}{\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}}\right) dx,$$

which `integrate()` evaluates to about $10^{-12}$. The bivariate density is written in
closed form.

```{r setup}
Phi2 <- function(a, b, rho) {
  if (a == -Inf || b == -Inf) return(0)
  if (a ==  Inf && b ==  Inf) return(1)
  if (a ==  Inf) return(pnorm(b))
  if (b ==  Inf) return(pnorm(a))
  s <- sqrt(1 - rho^2)
  integrate(function(x) dnorm(x) * pnorm((b - rho * x) / s),
            -Inf, a, rel.tol = 1e-12)$value
}

phi2 <- function(a, b, rho)
  exp(-(a^2 - 2 * rho * a * b + b^2) / (2 * (1 - rho^2))) /
  (2 * pi * sqrt(1 - rho^2))

# accuracy check against a closed-form value: Phi2(0,0;r) = 1/4 + asin(r)/(2*pi)
c(computed = Phi2(0, 0, 0.5), exact = 0.25 + asin(0.5) / (2 * pi))
```

In production, use `mvtnorm::pmvnorm`. One caveat worth pinning down before writing
tests that assert at $10^{-15}$: `pmvnorm`'s default algorithm uses randomised
quadrature, so repeated calls need not agree bit for bit. For two and three dimensions
`mvtnorm` also offers a deterministic routine, which is what a test suite wants.

This is illustration rather than code the document runs, so it is a plain fenced block
with no chunk engine attached:

```r
# production equivalent; check the algorithm argument before asserting tight tolerances
mvtnorm::pmvnorm(upper = c(a, b), corr = matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2),
                 algorithm = mvtnorm::TVPACK())
```

### Notation

Variable $j = 1,\dots,p$ has categories $0,\dots,K_j-1$ and thresholds
$\tau_{j,1} < \cdots < \tau_{j,K_j-1}$, with $\tau_{j,0} = -\infty$ and
$\tau_{j,K_j} = +\infty$. Write

$$q_{j,c} = P(Y_j < c) = \Phi(\tau_{j,c}), \qquad
  \pi_{j,c} = P(Y_j = c) = \Phi(\tau_{j,c+1}) - \Phi(\tau_{j,c}).$$

The cumulative convention $q_{j,c} = P(Y_j < c)$ is used internally throughout because
it makes $d\tau/dq = 1/\phi(\tau) > 0$ and removes a recurring minus sign.

Influence functions are normalised as

$$\sqrt{N}\,(\hat s - s) = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\psi_i + o_p(1),
  \qquad E(\psi_i) = 0, \qquad \Gamma = E(\psi_i\psi_i'),$$

so $\Gamma$ is $N$ times the asymptotic covariance of $\hat s$, matching what lavaan
documents as its `"gamma"` object.

### Running designs

```{r designs}
rho <- 0.50

# Design A: a binary pair
qA   <- c(0.30, 0.60)
tauA <- qnorm(qA)
p00  <- Phi2(tauA[1], tauA[2], rho)

# Design B: an ordinal pair, K = 4 and K = 3
pi1 <- c(0.15, 0.35, 0.30, 0.20)
pi2 <- c(0.40, 0.35, 0.25)
q1  <- cumsum(pi1)[-4];  t1 <- qnorm(q1)
q2  <- cumsum(pi2)[-3];  t2 <- qnorm(q2)
```

## Population model

Ordinal indicators arise by thresholding a bivariate standard normal:

$$\begin{pmatrix} Y_j^* \\ Y_k^* \end{pmatrix} \sim
  N\!\left[\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
  \begin{pmatrix}1 & \rho\\ \rho & 1\end{pmatrix}\right],
  \qquad Y_j = c \iff \tau_{j,c} < Y_j^* \le \tau_{j,c+1}.$$

Joint cell probabilities follow by rectangle differencing of the bivariate CDF:

$$P(Y_j = a, Y_k = b) =
  \Phi_2(\tau_{j,a+1},\tau_{k,b+1};\rho) - \Phi_2(\tau_{j,a},\tau_{k,b+1};\rho)
  - \Phi_2(\tau_{j,a+1},\tau_{k,b};\rho) + \Phi_2(\tau_{j,a},\tau_{k,b};\rho).$$

For $K_j = K_k = 2$ this reduces to the four-cell form
$p_{00} = \Phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho)$, $p_{01} = \Phi(\tau_1) - p_{00}$,
$p_{10} = \Phi(\tau_2) - p_{00}$, $p_{11} = 1 - \Phi(\tau_1) - \Phi(\tau_2) + p_{00}$.
Note $p_{10}$ marginalises $Y_j$ out and so carries $\Phi(\tau_2)$, not $\Phi(\tau_1)$.

### Identification

The parameter count decides whether the two-stage estimator coincides with joint ML.

| Pair | Free cells | Parameters | Status |
|------|-----------|-----------|--------|
| $2\times2$ | 3 | 3 | Saturated, just-identified |
| $K_j \times K_k$, either $>2$ | $K_jK_k - 1$ | $(K_j-1)+(K_k-1)+1$ | Over-identified |

In the saturated case the MLE reproduces the observed table exactly, hence its margins
exactly, hence $\Phi(\hat\tau_j) = \hat q_j$. Two-stage and joint ML therefore coincide
and $\hat\rho$ is a direct inversion. This is what makes the closed form of
@sec-oracle available for binary and for binary only.

## Stage 1: threshold influence functions

The estimator is the cumulative sample proportion pushed through the probit link,
$\hat\tau_{j,c} = \Phi^{-1}(\hat q_{j,c})$ with
$\hat q_{j,c} = N^{-1}\sum_i 1\{Y_{ji} < c\}$.

### Delta-method derivation

Let $Z_{j,c,i} = 1\{Y_{ji} < c\}$, so $E(Z_{j,c,i}) = q_{j,c}$. A sample proportion is an
ordinary mean, so $\psi_{q_{j,c},i} = Z_{j,c,i} - q_{j,c}$. Pushing through
$g(q) = \Phi^{-1}(q)$, whose derivative is $g'(q) = 1/\phi(\tau)$ by the inverse
function theorem,

$$\boxed{\;\psi_{\tau_{j,c},i} = \frac{1\{Y_{ji} < c\} - q_{j,c}}{\phi(\tau_{j,c})}\;}$$

Sign check: if the probability of falling below the threshold rises, $\hat q$ rises and
the estimated threshold must rise. Since $d\tau/dq = 1/\phi(\tau) > 0$, the sign is
right. Parameterising instead by $p = P(Y \ge c)$ gives $d\tau/dp = -1/\phi(\tau)$ and
the same influence function after substituting $p = 1-q$.

The variance follows from $Z_{j,c} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(q_{j,c})$:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{\tau_{j,c}}) =
  \frac{q_{j,c}(1-q_{j,c})}{\phi(\tau_{j,c})^{2}}.$$

### Staircase structure

Each influence function takes only two values and switches sign exactly once, at
$c = Y_{ji}$:

$$\psi_{\tau_{j,c},i} =
  \begin{cases}
    +\,(1-q_{j,c})\,/\,\phi(\tau_{j,c}), & Y_{ji} < c,\\[4pt]
    -\,q_{j,c}\,/\,\phi(\tau_{j,c}), & Y_{ji} \ge c.
  \end{cases}$$

```{r staircase}
psi_tau <- function(y, q) ((seq_along(q) > y) - q) / dnorm(qnorm(q))
staircase <- t(sapply(0:3, psi_tau, q = q1))
dimnames(staircase) <- list(paste("Y =", 0:3), paste0("psi[tau_", 1:3, "]"))
round(staircase, 4)
```

**Implementation consequence.** $\psi_j$ depends on $Y_{ji}$ only through which category
it fell in, so a variable with $K_j$ categories has exactly $K_j$ distinct influence
vectors. Build a $K_j \times (K_j-1)$ lookup table once and index it by the observed
category; no per-observation influence function is ever computed for the threshold
block.

Because $\hat q$ is the sample proportion, the estimated contributions have sample mean
exactly zero with no centring step. This is asserted in @sec-verify.

## Stage 1, second route: the ordered-probit score {#sec-score}

The same influence function drops out of the univariate likelihood by the M-estimator
formula at every $K$. This matters beyond confirmation: it establishes how the
score-and-Hessian machinery attaches to the first-stage result, which is the apparatus
Stage 2 needs.

### Binary case

With $Z_i = 1\{Y_{ji} = 0\}$,

$$\ell_i(\tau) = Z_i\log\Phi(\tau) + (1-Z_i)\log(1-\Phi(\tau)),
  \qquad s_i(\tau) = \frac{\phi(\tau)(Z_i - q)}{q(1-q)}.$$

Differentiating the score, the term multiplying $(Z_i - q)$ vanishes in expectation at
the true $\tau$, leaving only the derivative that hits $-\Phi(\tau)$:

$$A = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial s_i}{\partial\tau}\right] = \frac{\phi(\tau)^2}{q(1-q)},
  \qquad
  \psi_i = A^{-1}s_i = \frac{q(1-q)}{\phi^2}\cdot\frac{\phi(Z_i-q)}{q(1-q)}
         = \frac{Z_i - q}{\phi(\tau)}.$$

Further, $B = \operatorname{Var}(s_i) = \phi^2/[q(1-q)] = A$, so the sandwich
$A^{-1}BA^{-1}$ collapses to $A^{-1}$. The information-matrix equality holds:
$\Phi^{-1}(\hat q)$ is the MLE by invariance, not merely a convenient moment estimator.

```{r score-binary}
q <- qA[1]; tt <- tauA[1]
A  <- dnorm(tt)^2 / (q * (1 - q))
s  <- dnorm(tt) * (c(1, 0) - q) / (q * (1 - q))   # score at Z = 1 and Z = 0
B  <- q * s[1]^2 + (1 - q) * s[2]^2
data.frame(
  quantity = c("psi | Z=1", "psi | Z=0", "asymptotic variance"),
  score_route = c(s / A, B / A^2),
  delta_route = c((1 - q) / dnorm(tt), -q / dnorm(tt), q * (1 - q) / dnorm(tt)^2)
)
```

### General $K$: a tridiagonal system

For $K > 2$ the score is a $(K_j-1)$-dimensional system in which $\tau_c$ enters only
the two cells it borders:

$$s_c = \phi(\tau_c)\left[\frac{1\{Y = c-1\}}{\pi_{c-1}} - \frac{1\{Y = c\}}{\pi_c}\right].$$

Adjacent thresholds share a cell and non-adjacent ones do not, so the information
matrix is tridiagonal:

$$A_{cc} = \phi(\tau_c)^2\!\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{c-1}} + \frac{1}{\pi_c}\right),\quad
  A_{c,c+1} = -\frac{\phi(\tau_c)\phi(\tau_{c+1})}{\pi_c},\quad
  A_{cd} = 0 \ \text{ for } |c-d| > 1.$$

So $\psi = A^{-1}s$ now requires inverting a genuine system, and there is no a priori
reason it should collapse back to the simple per-threshold form. It does, exactly.
Equivalently, the inverse of that tridiagonal matrix has the min structure

$$\left(A^{-1}\right)_{cd} =
  \frac{q_{c\wedge d}\left(1 - q_{c\vee d}\right)}{\phi(\tau_c)\,\phi(\tau_d)},$$

the Green's-function form characteristic of tridiagonal matrices. This is why Stage 1
stays cheap: the implementation never forms or inverts $A$, it reads off cumulative
proportions.

```{r score-general}
info_tri <- function(tau, pmf) {
  m <- length(tau); d <- dnorm(tau); A <- matrix(0, m, m)
  for (c in seq_len(m)) {
    A[c, c] <- d[c]^2 * (1 / pmf[c] + 1 / pmf[c + 1])
    if (c < m) A[c, c + 1] <- A[c + 1, c] <- -d[c] * d[c + 1] / pmf[c + 1]
  }
  A
}
score <- function(y, tau, pmf) {
  d <- dnorm(tau)
  sapply(seq_along(tau), function(c) d[c] * ((y == c - 1) / pmf[c] - (y == c) / pmf[c + 1]))
}

A1 <- info_tri(t1, pi1)
round(A1, 6)
```

**Efficiency.** Because the information-matrix equality holds at every $K$, the
within-variable block of $\Gamma$ is exactly the inverse univariate information. Stage 1
loses no efficiency regardless of the number of categories.

## The threshold block of $\Gamma$ {#sec-gamma}

One formula covers every entry of the $T \times T$ threshold block, where
$T = \sum_j (K_j - 1)$:

$$\boxed{\;\Gamma_{(j,c),(k,d)} =
  \frac{P(Y_j < c,\ Y_k < d) - q_{j,c}\,q_{k,d}}
       {\phi(\tau_{j,c})\,\phi(\tau_{k,d})}\;}$$

Only the joint probability changes between the two cases:

$$P(Y_j<c,\ Y_k<d) =
  \begin{cases}
    \min(q_{j,c},\,q_{j,d}), & j = k,\\[4pt]
    \Phi_2(\tau_{j,c},\,\tau_{k,d};\,\rho_{jk}), & j \neq k.
  \end{cases}$$

For $j=k$ and $c<d$ this reduces to $q_{j,c}(1-q_{j,d})$, which is strictly positive:
thresholds within a variable are **always** positively correlated, whatever $\rho$ is.
Setting $c=d$ recovers the diagonal $q(1-q)/\phi^2$. For $j \neq k$ the entry is zero at
$\rho_{jk}=0$, positive above and negative below, so the block is already non-diagonal
before the polychoric correlations enter the statistics vector at all.

**Cost bound.** No entry of the threshold block ever requires more than a bivariate
normal CDF, at any $K$ and any number of variables. This is not obvious a priori, and it
is worth having settled before the $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\rho_{jk},\hat\rho_{lm})$
entries, which are where higher-dimensional integrals would otherwise appear.

```{r gamma-fn}
gamma_tau <- function(tau, q, var_id, rho_mat) {
  P <- length(tau)
  outer(seq_len(P), seq_len(P), Vectorize(function(a, b) {
    joint <- if (var_id[a] == var_id[b]) min(q[a], q[b])
             else Phi2(tau[a], tau[b], rho_mat[var_id[a], var_id[b]])
    (joint - q[a] * q[b]) / (dnorm(tau[a]) * dnorm(tau[b]))
  }))
}

tau_all <- c(t1, t2); q_all <- c(q1, q2); var_id <- c(rep(1, 3), rep(2, 2))
R_mat   <- matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2)
G       <- gamma_tau(tau_all, q_all, var_id, R_mat)
round(G, 6)
```

### The within-variable block needs no estimation

For a single variable the analytic and empirical constructions are not merely close —
they are the same arithmetic. The product of two cumulative indicators on the same
variable collapses,

$$Z_{j,c}\,Z_{j,d} = 1\{Y_j < c\}\,1\{Y_j < d\} = 1\{Y_j < \min(c,d)\},$$

so the sample mean of the product is $\hat q_{j,\min(c,d)}$ *exactly*. The empirical
entry is therefore

$$\frac1N\sum_i \hat\psi_{a,i}\hat\psi_{b,i}
  = \frac{\overline{Z_aZ_b} - \hat q_a\hat q_b}{\phi(\hat\tau_a)\phi(\hat\tau_b)}
  = \frac{\min(\hat q_a,\hat q_b) - \hat q_a\hat q_b}
         {\phi(\hat\tau_a)\phi(\hat\tau_b)},$$

which is the analytic formula evaluated at the estimated thresholds. This holds for any
sample at any $N$, not asymptotically.

Two consequences. First, all of the discrepancy between an empirical and an analytic
$\Gamma$ lives in the cross-variable entries, where $\overline{Z_aZ_b}$ *estimates*
$\Phi_2$ rather than equalling it. Second, the corresponding unit test should assert
machine precision rather than a tolerance: a failure in the within-variable block is a
coding error, never sampling noise. Asserted in @sec-verify.

### Why this is a test oracle, not the production path

The cross-variable entries depend on $\rho_{jk}$, so the analytic $\Gamma_{\tau\tau}$
cannot be assembled until Stage 2 has run. The empirical construction
$\hat\Gamma = N^{-1}\sum_i \hat\psi_i\hat\psi_i'$ has no such ordering problem, and it
picks up the cross-pair correlation covariances for free rather than requiring them in
closed form. Production uses the empirical outer product; the formulas above are unit
tests.

## Verification {#sec-verify}

```{r verify-helpers}
tol_report <- function(label, observed, threshold)
  data.frame(check = label,
             observed = format(observed, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE),
             threshold = format(threshold, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE),
             pass = observed < threshold)
```

### Exact identities

These involve no simulation and no numerical integration, so they should hold to machine
precision.

```{r verify-exact}
d1 <- max(abs(solve(A1) - G[1:3, 1:3]))
d2 <- max(sapply(0:3, function(y)
        max(abs(solve(A1, score(y, t1, pi1)) - psi_tau(y, q1)))))

rbind(
  tol_report("tridiagonal A^-1 equals the within-variable block", d1, 1e-12),
  tol_report("A^-1 s equals psi, all category values",           d2, 1e-12)
)
```

### Empirical $\hat\Gamma$ against the analytic form

```{r verify-empirical}
set.seed(917)
draw_pair <- function(n) {
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n), n, 2) %*% chol(matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2))
  cbind(findInterval(Z[, 1], t1), findInterval(Z[, 2], t2))
}
cum_ind <- function(Y) cbind(outer(Y[, 1], 1:3, "<"), outer(Y[, 2], 1:2, "<")) * 1

N  <- 200000
Zc <- cum_ind(draw_pair(N))
qh <- colMeans(Zc)
psi_hat <- sweep(Zc, 2, qh) / rep(dnorm(qnorm(qh)), each = N)

rbind(
  tol_report(sprintf("max |Gamma-hat - Gamma|, N = %d", N),
             max(abs(crossprod(psi_hat) / N - G)), 0.05),
  tol_report("column means of psi-hat are exactly zero",
             max(abs(colMeans(psi_hat))), 1e-12)
)
```

### Monte Carlo covariance of $\hat\tau$

The finite-sample covariance of $\hat\tau$ sits slightly above $\Gamma/N$ because of the
$O(N^{-1})$ curvature term in the delta expansion of $\Phi^{-1}$ around a proportion.
That term shrinks with $N$, not with the number of replications.

Raw percentage deviations are not a usable criterion here: the small off-diagonal
entries carry large relative Monte Carlo error, so the worst percentage in the matrix is
dominated by noise rather than by any discrepancy. The check is therefore reported as a
$z$ statistic against each entry's own Monte Carlo standard error, using
$\operatorname{SE}(\hat\sigma_{ab}) \approx
\sqrt{(\sigma_{aa}\sigma_{bb} + \sigma_{ab}^2)/R}$. With 15 distinct entries, the
largest $|z|$ should land near 2.5 and a threshold of 4 is the sensible bound.

The curvature term is reported separately, as the mean relative excess on the diagonal,
where it is the quantity of interest rather than noise. It should be positive and should
fall as `N_mc` rises.

```{r verify-mc}
#| cache: true
set.seed(4242)
N_mc <- 3000; R_mc <- 2000
TH <- t(replicate(R_mc, qnorm(colMeans(cum_ind(draw_pair(N_mc))))))

C  <- cov(TH) * N_mc
se <- outer(seq_len(ncol(TH)), seq_len(ncol(TH)),
            Vectorize(function(a, b) sqrt((C[a, a] * C[b, b] + C[a, b]^2) / R_mc)))
z  <- abs(C - G) / se

data.frame(max_abs_z         = round(max(z), 2),
           pass              = max(z) < 4,
           curvature_bias_pct = round(100 * mean(diag(C) / diag(G) - 1), 2))
```

### Two-stage against joint ML

For the saturated $2\times2$ table the two estimators must coincide exactly. For the
over-identified $4\times3$ table they must not.

The $2\times2$ residual below is not zero, but it is Nelder-Mead's convergence
tolerance rather than a real difference; what carries the argument is that the
$4\times3$ gap is roughly two orders of magnitude larger on a table built the same way
and perturbed the same way. The $4\times3$ gap is small in absolute terms only because
the table was generated from the model and lightly perturbed — it is a function of fit,
and grows under misspecification.

```{r verify-ml}
#| cache: true
cell_probs <- function(a, b, r) {
  A <- c(-Inf, a, Inf); B <- c(-Inf, b, Inf)
  outer(seq_len(length(a) + 1), seq_len(length(b) + 1), Vectorize(function(i, j)
    Phi2(A[i + 1], B[j + 1], r) - Phi2(A[i], B[j + 1], r) -
    Phi2(A[i + 1], B[j], r)     + Phi2(A[i], B[j], r)))
}

# thresholds are parameterised as (first, log-increments) so ordering is automatic;
# a single threshold (the binary case) is passed through unchanged
unpack <- function(v) if (length(v) == 1) v else cumsum(c(v[1], exp(v[-1])))

joint_ml <- function(tab) {
  n1 <- nrow(tab) - 1; n2 <- ncol(tab) - 1
  nll <- function(p)
    -sum(tab * log(pmax(cell_probs(unpack(p[seq_len(n1)]),
                                   unpack(p[n1 + seq_len(n2)]),
                                   tanh(p[n1 + n2 + 1])), 1e-14)))
  o <- optim(numeric(n1 + n2 + 1), nll, method = "Nelder-Mead",
             control = list(maxit = 20000, reltol = 1e-12))
  list(t1 = unpack(o$par[seq_len(n1)]), t2 = unpack(o$par[n1 + seq_len(n2)]),
       rho = tanh(o$par[n1 + n2 + 1]))
}
two_stage_tau <- function(tab)
  list(t1 = qnorm(cumsum(rowSums(tab) / sum(tab))[-nrow(tab)]),
       t2 = qnorm(cumsum(colSums(tab) / sum(tab))[-ncol(tab)]))

# saturated 2 x 2
tab2 <- round(cell_probs(tauA[1], tauA[2], rho) * 2e5) + matrix(c(311, -52, 8, -93), 2)
ml2  <- joint_ml(tab2); ts2 <- two_stage_tau(tab2)

# over-identified 4 x 3
tab4 <- round(cell_probs(t1, t2, rho) * 2e5)
tab4[1, 1] <- tab4[1, 1] + 311; tab4[3, 2] <- tab4[3, 2] - 274
ml4  <- joint_ml(tab4); ts4 <- two_stage_tau(tab4)

gap2 <- max(abs(c(ml2$t1 - ts2$t1, ml2$t2 - ts2$t2)))
gap4 <- max(abs(c(ml4$t1 - ts4$t1, ml4$t2 - ts4$t2)))

data.frame(
  table           = c("2 x 2 (saturated)", "4 x 3 (over-identified)"),
  max_abs_tau_gap = c(gap2, gap4),
  expectation     = c("optimizer tolerance only", "structurally non-zero"),
  ratio_to_2x2    = c(1, round(gap4 / gap2, 1))
)
```

### More than two variables

Everything above exercises a single pair. The threshold block for $p > 2$ brings in
structure a pair cannot show: blocks that must repeat where the design repeats, and a
matrix that must stay positive definite once cross-variable entries at several different
correlations are present. Four indicators from a one-factor model with
$\lambda = 0.7$ (so $\rho_{jk} = 0.49$ for every pair) give $T = 3+3+2+2 = 10$.

```{r verify-multivariable}
#| cache: true
lambda <- 0.7
R4   <- matrix(lambda^2, 4, 4); diag(R4) <- 1
thr4 <- list(t1, t1, t2, t2)                       # reuse the running designs
tau4 <- unlist(thr4); q4 <- pnorm(tau4)
vid4 <- rep(1:4, lengths(thr4))
lab4 <- unlist(lapply(1:4, function(j) paste0("y", j, "|t", seq_along(thr4[[j]]))))

G4 <- gamma_tau(tau4, q4, vid4, R4); dimnames(G4) <- list(lab4, lab4)

set.seed(202)
n4   <- 300000
f4   <- rnorm(n4)
Y4   <- sapply(1:4, function(j)
          findInterval(lambda * f4 + sqrt(1 - lambda^2) * rnorm(n4), thr4[[j]]))
Z4   <- do.call(cbind, lapply(1:4, function(j)
          outer(Y4[, j], seq_along(thr4[[j]]), "<"))) * 1
qh4  <- colMeans(Z4)
psi4 <- sweep(Z4, 2, qh4) / rep(dnorm(qnorm(qh4)), each = n4)

data.frame(
  check = c("min eigenvalue of Gamma (must exceed 0)",
            "y1 block equals y2 block (identical thresholds)",
            "y1~y3 block equals y2~y4 block (identical pair geometry)",
            sprintf("max |Gamma-hat - Gamma|, N = %s",
                    format(n4, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE))),
  result = c(format(min(eigen(G4, only.values = TRUE)$values), digits = 4),
             isTRUE(all.equal(G4[1:3, 1:3],  G4[4:6, 4:6],   check.attributes = FALSE)),
             isTRUE(all.equal(G4[1:3, 7:8],  G4[4:6, 9:10],  check.attributes = FALSE)),
             format(max(abs(crossprod(psi4) / n4 - G4)), digits = 3))
)
```

### The within-variable identity

The claim of @sec-gamma is that within a variable the empirical and analytic blocks are
identical arithmetic, not merely close. The gap below should be machine precision at
every sample size, growing only with floating-point accumulation in the crossproduct.

```{r verify-identity}
identity_gap <- function(n) {
  f  <- rnorm(n)
  Y  <- sapply(1:4, function(j)
          findInterval(lambda * f + sqrt(1 - lambda^2) * rnorm(n), thr4[[j]]))
  Z  <- do.call(cbind, lapply(1:4, function(j)
          outer(Y[, j], seq_along(thr4[[j]]), "<"))) * 1
  qh <- colMeans(Z); th <- qnorm(qh)
  ps <- sweep(Z, 2, qh) / rep(dnorm(th), each = n)
  w  <- outer(vid4, vid4, "==")
  max(abs((crossprod(ps) / n - gamma_tau(th, qh, vid4, R4))[w]))
}

set.seed(7)
ns <- c(200, 5000, 100000)
data.frame(n = format(ns, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE),
           max_within_variable_gap = format(sapply(ns, identity_gap), digits = 3))
```

### Cross-check against lavaan

The most valuable external validation is lavaan's own $\Gamma$. This chunk has never been
executed: CRAN is unreachable from the sandbox this file was written in, so it is
untested code and should be read as a starting point rather than a working check.

Two things in it are deliberately left open. The model uses four indicators because a
single-factor model on two indicators is not identified. And the ordering of lavaan's
$\Gamma$ is asserted nowhere below — this document's convention is thresholds by
variable then index, followed by lower-triangle correlations, and lavaan is believed to
match, but that has not been confirmed against actual output. Check it before trusting
any element-wise comparison.

```{r lavaan-check}
#| eval: false
library(lavaan)

set.seed(11)
n <- 5000; lambda <- 0.7
f     <- rnorm(n)
Ystar <- sapply(1:4, function(j) lambda * f + sqrt(1 - lambda^2) * rnorm(n))
thr   <- list(t1, t1, t2, t2)            # reuse the running designs
dat   <- as.data.frame(lapply(1:4, function(j)
           ordered(findInterval(Ystar[, j], thr[[j]]))))
names(dat) <- paste0("y", 1:4)

fit <- lavaan::sem("f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4", data = dat,
                   ordered = names(dat), estimator = "DWLS")

lav_gamma  <- lavInspect(fit, "gamma")
lav_labels <- names(lavInspect(fit, "wls.obs"))

# Alignment is settled: Gamma is 16 x 16 = T + n_pairs, labelled
#   y1|t1 y1|t2 y1|t3 y2|t1 y2|t2 y2|t3 y3|t1 y3|t2 y4|t1 y4|t2 | y1~~y2 ... y3~~y4
# i.e. thresholds first, variable-major with ascending threshold index, then
# correlations in column-major lower-triangle order -- this document's convention
# exactly. No permutation is needed. Indexing below is still by name, not position,
# so the comparison stays correct if a future lavaan changes the order.

thr_lab <- grep("|", lav_labels, fixed = TRUE, value = TRUE)

th_hat  <- lavInspect(fit, "th")[thr_lab]       # thresholds, as lavaan estimated them
rho_hat <- lavInspect(fit, "sampstat")$cov      # polychoric correlations
var_id  <- match(sub("\\|.*$", "", thr_lab), rownames(rho_hat))

G_ana <- gamma_tau(th_hat, pnorm(th_hat), var_id, rho_hat)
G_lav <- lav_gamma[thr_lab, thr_lab]

max(abs(G_ana - G_lav))
```

#### Result, and how to read it

Run on the design above at $n = 5000$, this returned **0.0580**. That is agreement, and
it identifies how lavaan builds $\hat\Gamma$.

The reference distribution was obtained by simulating the same comparison 300 times at
$n = 5000$ — empirical outer product against the analytic formula at the same estimated
thresholds. The maximum absolute gap has median 0.0565, interquartile range
[0.0492, 0.0659], and a 90% interval of [0.0394, 0.0873]. The observed 0.0580 sits at
the **55th percentile**: as close to the centre of the expected distribution as one
could reasonably ask.

For a second, independent opinion, the analytic standard error of the single noisiest
entry — the $y_1|t_1$ diagonal, where $q = 0.15$ makes $\psi$ most skewed — is 0.0650 at
$n = 5000$, on its own larger than the observed maximum across all 100 entries.

The diagnosis this settles: **lavaan builds $\hat\Gamma$ empirically, by averaging
estimated influence functions, not by plugging estimates into a closed form.** Had it
used the analytic plug-in, the gap would have been machine precision, because the
identity of @sec-gamma makes the within-variable block exact and the cross-variable
entries would then have been the same formula on both sides.

Two caveats on the comparison itself. Both sides are evaluated at estimates rather than
population values, so exact equality was never the target. And two assumptions in the
chunk remain unverified: that `lavInspect(fit, "th")` returns a vector named to match
`thr_lab`, and that under the delta parameterization with no covariates lavaan's
thresholds sit on the same standardized scale used here. Neither is implicated by a
result this well-centred, but both would matter if the design changed.

What would have been a real mismatch: a gap that is structural rather than stochastic —
a constant factor, a transposed block, or a discrepancy concentrated in the
within-variable entries, which by @sec-gamma should be exact regardless of $n$.

## Stage 2: the $2\times2$ oracle {#sec-oracle}

The binary case admits a closed form, derived here by a route independent of the general
argument in @sec-general. Keeping it as its own section is deliberate: two derivations
reaching the same expression is corroboration, and collapsing it into the general result
would throw that away.

Because the binary pair is saturated, $\hat\rho$ is a smooth function of the trivariate
sample mean $(\hat q_1, \hat q_2, \hat p_{00})$, defined implicitly by
$\Phi_2(\Phi^{-1}(q_1), \Phi^{-1}(q_2); \rho) = p_{00}$. Two derivatives are needed —
Plackett's identity for $\rho$, and the usual partial for each threshold:

$$\frac{\partial \Phi_2}{\partial \rho} = \phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho), \qquad
  \frac{\partial \Phi_2}{\partial \tau_1} =
  \phi(\tau_1)\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\tau_2 - \rho\tau_1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right).$$

Applying the implicit function theorem, the $\phi(\tau_j)$ arriving from
$d\tau_j/dq_j$ cancels:

$$\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial q_1} =
  -\frac{\Phi\!\left(\frac{\tau_2-\rho\tau_1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)}
        {\phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho)}, \qquad
  \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial q_2} =
  -\frac{\Phi\!\left(\frac{\tau_1-\rho\tau_2}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)}
        {\phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho)}, \qquad
  \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial p_{00}} = \frac{1}{\phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho)}.$$

Hence

$$\boxed{\;\psi_{\rho,i} = \frac{1}{\phi_2(\tau_1,\tau_2;\rho)}
  \left[\big(1\{Y_{1i}<1,\,Y_{2i}<1\} - p_{00}\big)
  - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{\tau_2-\rho\tau_1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)\big(1\{Y_{1i}<1\}-q_1\big)
  - \Phi\!\left(\tfrac{\tau_1-\rho\tau_2}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)\big(1\{Y_{2i}<1\}-q_2\big)
  \right]\;}$$

The structure is the expected one: a direct term in the joint cell, minus two
first-stage correction terms, each weighted by a conditional normal probability. The
weight on the $q_1$ correction is $P(Y_2^* \le \tau_2 \mid Y_1^* = \tau_1)$, the rate at
which a shift in the first threshold propagates into the joint cell.

```{r oracle}
s   <- sqrt(1 - rho^2)
d2v <- phi2(tauA[1], tauA[2], rho)
grad <- c(q1  = -pnorm((tauA[2] - rho * tauA[1]) / s) / d2v,
          q2  = -pnorm((tauA[1] - rho * tauA[2]) / s) / d2v,
          p00 =  1 / d2v)

rho_of <- function(a, b, c)
  uniroot(function(r) Phi2(qnorm(a), qnorm(b), r) - c, c(-0.999, 0.999), tol = 1e-12)$root

h <- 1e-5
numeric_grad <- c(
  (rho_of(qA[1] + h, qA[2], p00) - rho_of(qA[1] - h, qA[2], p00)) / (2 * h),
  (rho_of(qA[1], qA[2] + h, p00) - rho_of(qA[1], qA[2] - h, p00)) / (2 * h),
  (rho_of(qA[1], qA[2], p00 + h) - rho_of(qA[1], qA[2], p00 - h)) / (2 * h))

data.frame(derivative = names(grad), analytic = grad, numeric = numeric_grad,
           row.names = NULL)
```

```{r oracle-variance}
#| cache: true
V <- matrix(c(qA[1] * (1 - qA[1]), p00 - qA[1] * qA[2],  p00 - qA[1] * p00,
              p00 - qA[1] * qA[2], qA[2] * (1 - qA[2]),  p00 - qA[2] * p00,
              p00 - qA[1] * p00,   p00 - qA[2] * p00,    p00 * (1 - p00)), 3, 3)
implied <- drop(grad %*% V %*% grad)

set.seed(99)
N_r <- 4000; R_r <- 1500
rh <- replicate(R_r, {
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(2 * N_r), N_r, 2) %*% chol(matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2))
  a <- Z[, 1] <= tauA[1]; b <- Z[, 2] <= tauA[2]
  rho_of(mean(a), mean(b), mean(a & b))
})
mc  <- var(rh) * N_r
se  <- mc * sqrt(2 / (R_r - 1))

data.frame(implied_N_var = implied, monte_carlo = mc, mc_std_error = se,
           z = abs(mc - implied) / se)
```

### How this relates to the general case

For $K > 2$ the pair is over-identified, so $\hat\rho$ is not an inversion but the root
of the pairwise conditional score given $\hat\tau$, and the influence function comes
from the M-estimator formula of @sec-score rather than from an implicit-function
cancellation. That derivation is @sec-general. Its acceptance test was that it reduce to
the boxed expression above at $K_1 = K_2 = 2$; it does, to 7e-15 across sixty
combinations of $(q_1, q_2, \rho)$ — verified in @sec-general's Level 5.

The two routes are worth contrasting. Here the saturation of the $2\times2$ table makes
$\hat\rho$ an explicit function of three sample proportions, so the delta method
suffices and the threshold correction appears as a conditional normal probability. There
no such explicit function exists, and the correction appears instead as a ratio of
expected informations. That they agree is not a foregone conclusion, and it is the
strongest evidence available that neither derivation has a sign or indexing error.

## Stage 2, general case: the $K > 2$ influence function {#sec-general}

This closes Gate 3. The result is stated first, then derived, then verified.

$$\boxed{\;\psi_{\rho,i} = \frac{1}{I_{\rho\rho}}
\left[\,u_{r_i s_i} \;-\; \sum_c I_{\rho a_c}\,\psi_{a_c,i}
                     \;-\; \sum_d I_{\rho b_d}\,\psi_{b_d,i}\right]\;}$$

where $(r_i,s_i)$ is the cell observation $i$ falls in, $u_{rs} =
\partial_\rho\pi_{rs}/\pi_{rs}$, and

$$I_{\rho\rho} = \sum_{rs}\frac{(\partial_\rho\pi_{rs})^2}{\pi_{rs}},
\qquad
I_{\rho a_c} = \sum_{rs}\frac{(\partial_\rho\pi_{rs})(\partial_{a_c}\pi_{rs})}{\pi_{rs}}.$$

### The estimating system

Variable $j$ has thresholds $a_1 < \dots < a_{K_1-1}$ with $a_0 = -\infty$,
$a_{K_1} = \infty$; variable $k$ has $b_1 < \dots < b_{K_2-1}$. Cell
probabilities come from rectangle differencing of the bivariate CDF,

$$\pi_{rs} = \Phi_2(a_{r+1},b_{s+1};\rho) - \Phi_2(a_r,b_{s+1};\rho)
           - \Phi_2(a_{r+1},b_s;\rho)   + \Phi_2(a_r,b_s;\rho).$$

Stage 2 holds $\hat a, \hat b$ fixed and solves the pairwise score equation.
The per-observation contribution is

$$g_i(\rho, a, b) = \sum_{rs} \mathbb 1\{Y_j = r,\, Y_k = s\}\; u_{rs},
\qquad u_{rs} = \frac{\partial_\rho \pi_{rs}}{\pi_{rs}},$$

which has mean zero at the truth because $\sum_{rs}\partial_\rho\pi_{rs} =
\partial_\rho(1) = 0$.

### The two-step expansion

Expanding $0 = N^{-1}\sum_i g_i(\hat\rho,\hat a,\hat b)$ about $(\rho,a,b)$
and substituting $\hat a_c - a_c = N^{-1}\sum_i \psi_{a_c,i} + o_p(N^{-1/2})$
gives the standard two-step M-estimator form,

$$\psi_{\rho,i} = \frac{1}{A}\left[g_i + \sum_c G_{a_c}\psi_{a_c,i}
                                       + \sum_d G_{b_d}\psi_{b_d,i}\right],
\qquad A = -E\!\left[\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial\rho}\right],
\quad G_{a_c} = E\!\left[\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial a_c}\right].$$

Both expectations collapse, and for the same reason in each case: the term
carrying a second derivative of $\pi$ sums to $\partial(1) = 0$ over the
table. For $A$,

$$E\!\left[\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial\rho}\right]
= \sum_{rs}\partial^2_\rho\pi_{rs}
 -\sum_{rs}\frac{(\partial_\rho\pi_{rs})^2}{\pi_{rs}}
= -\,I_{\rho\rho},$$

and identically for the cross term, $G_{a_c} = -I_{\rho a_c}$. Substituting
gives the boxed result, and with it the sensitivity the spec's chain-rule
sketch asks for:

$$\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial a_c} = -\frac{I_{\rho a_c}}{I_{\rho\rho}}.$$

### The derivatives, in closed form

Plackett's identity gives $\partial_\rho\Phi_2 = \phi_2$, so
$\partial_\rho\pi_{rs}$ is the same rectangle difference taken on the
bivariate *density* at the cell's four corners, with $\phi_2(\pm\infty,\cdot)
= 0$.

The threshold derivative is sparser than it looks: $a_c$ appears in exactly
two rows of the table, the ones it separates. Writing

$$w_{c,s} = \phi(a_c)\left[\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{b_{s+1}-\rho a_c}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)
                          -\Phi\!\left(\tfrac{b_s    -\rho a_c}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\right)\right]$$

— the joint density of $Y_j^* = a_c$ with $Y_k$ in category $s$ — we get
$\partial_{a_c}\pi_{c-1,s} = w_{c,s}$, $\partial_{a_c}\pi_{c,s} = -w_{c,s}$,
and zero in every other row. Hence the compact form

$$I_{\rho a_c} = \sum_s w_{c,s}\,\big(u_{c-1,s} - u_{c,s}\big),$$

a sum over one variable's categories rather than the whole table. This is the
$K>2$ analogue of the tridiagonal sparsity in @sec-score: a threshold only
ever couples to its two neighbouring cells.

### Two consequences for the implementation

**$\psi_\rho$ is a lookup table.** It depends on observation $i$ only through
its cell $(r_i,s_i)$ — the threshold influence functions are themselves
category lookups, so the whole thing is a $K_1 \times K_2$ table per pair,
built once. Combined with the staircase result of @sec-verify, **no
per-observation influence function is computed anywhere in Γ's construction**,
at either stage.

**Module 2 does not need numerical second derivatives.** The spec anticipated
handing Module 4 the Hessian of the bivariate log-likelihood. It turns out
everything required is closed-form in $\pi$ and its *first* derivatives:
$I_{\rho\rho}$ and $I_{\rho a_c}$ are expected informations, computable from
the cell probabilities and the corner densities alone. So Module 2's
obligation is lighter than expected. It must return, per pair:

| Quantity | Shape | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| $\hat\rho_{jk}$ | scalar | the statistic vector $s$ |
| $u_{rs}$ | $K_1 \times K_2$ | the direct term |
| $I_{\rho\rho}$ | scalar | the normalisation |
| $I_{\rho a_c}$, $I_{\rho b_d}$ | $K_1-1$, $K_2-1$ | the propagation weights |

Module 4 combines those with the Stage 1 threshold influence functions. The
boundary stays where spec §5 puts it: Module 2 estimates, Module 4 assembles.

### Verification

Built in levels so that a failure localises rather than merely reporting that
something is wrong.

```{r gate3-core}
#| cache: true
phi2s <- function(x, y, rho)                      # guarded at infinities
  if (!is.finite(x) || !is.finite(y)) 0 else phi2(x, y, rho)

cellP <- function(a, b, rho) {                    # each corner computed once
  A <- c(-Inf, a, Inf); B <- c(-Inf, b, Inf)
  C <- outer(seq_along(A), seq_along(B), Vectorize(function(r,s) Phi2(A[r],B[s],rho)))
  C[-1,-1] - C[-nrow(C),-1] - C[-1,-ncol(C)] + C[-nrow(C),-ncol(C)]
}
dP_drho <- function(a, b, rho) {
  A <- c(-Inf, a, Inf); B <- c(-Inf, b, Inf)
  outer(seq_len(length(a)+1), seq_len(length(b)+1), Vectorize(function(r,s)
    phi2s(A[r+1],B[s+1],rho) - phi2s(A[r],B[s+1],rho) -
    phi2s(A[r+1],B[s],  rho) + phi2s(A[r],B[s],  rho)))
}
wmat <- function(a, b, rho) {
  s <- sqrt(1-rho^2); B <- c(-Inf, b, Inf)
  outer(seq_along(a), seq_len(length(b)+1), Vectorize(function(c,t)
    dnorm(a[c]) * (pnorm((B[t+1]-rho*a[c])/s) - pnorm((B[t]-rho*a[c])/s))))
}
dP_da <- function(a, b, rho, c) {
  W <- wmat(a,b,rho); M <- matrix(0, length(a)+1, length(b)+1)
  M[c,] <- W[c,]; M[c+1,] <- -W[c,]; M
}
dP_db <- function(a, b, rho, d) t(dP_da(b, a, rho, d))

info <- function(a, b, rho) {
  P <- cellP(a,b,rho); Pr <- dP_drho(a,b,rho)
  list(P = P, u = Pr/P, Irr = sum(Pr^2/P),
       Ira = sapply(seq_along(a), function(c) sum(Pr*dP_da(a,b,rho,c)/P)),
       Irb = sapply(seq_along(b), function(d) sum(Pr*dP_db(a,b,rho,d)/P)))
}

psi_rho_table <- function(a, b, rho, drop_propagation = FALSE) {
  I <- info(a,b,rho); K1 <- length(a)+1; K2 <- length(b)+1
  qa <- pnorm(a); qb <- pnorm(b)
  psi_a <- outer(seq_len(K1), seq_along(a), function(r,c) ((r <= c) - qa[c])/dnorm(a[c]))
  psi_b <- outer(seq_len(K2), seq_along(b), function(s,d) ((s <= d) - qb[d])/dnorm(b[d]))
  corr <- if (drop_propagation) matrix(0, K1, K2) else
          outer(seq_len(K1), seq_len(K2), Vectorize(function(r,s)
            sum(I$Ira*psi_a[r,]) + sum(I$Irb*psi_b[s,])))
  (I$u - corr) / I$Irr
}
```

**Level 1 — the derivatives of $\pi$.** Everything downstream is built from
these, so they are checked against numerical differentiation first.

```{r gate3-L1}
#| cache: true
h <- 1e-5
g1 <- max(abs(dP_drho(t1,t2,rho) - (cellP(t1,t2,rho+h) - cellP(t1,t2,rho-h))/(2*h)))
g2 <- max(sapply(seq_along(t1), function(c) {
  ap <- t1; ap[c] <- ap[c]+h; am <- t1; am[c] <- am[c]-h
  max(abs(dP_da(t1,t2,rho,c) - (cellP(ap,t2,rho)-cellP(am,t2,rho))/(2*h))) }))
g3 <- max(sapply(seq_along(t2), function(d) {
  bp <- t2; bp[d] <- bp[d]+h; bm <- t2; bm[d] <- bm[d]-h
  max(abs(dP_db(t1,t2,rho,d) - (cellP(t1,bp,rho)-cellP(t1,bm,rho))/(2*h))) }))
data.frame(check = c("d pi / d rho", "d pi / d a_c", "d pi / d b_d",
                     "cells sum to 1", "d/drho sums to 0"),
           value = format(c(g1, g2, g3, sum(cellP(t1,t2,rho)) - 1,
                            sum(dP_drho(t1,t2,rho))), digits = 3))
```

**Level 2 — the information quantities**, against numerical differentiation of
$E[g]$ with the true cell probabilities held fixed, plus the $w$-weighted form
against the direct sum.

```{r gate3-L2}
#| cache: true
Ptrue <- cellP(t1, t2, rho)
Eg <- function(aa, bb, rr) sum(Ptrue * (dP_drho(aa,bb,rr) / cellP(aa,bb,rr)))
I  <- info(t1, t2, rho)

num_a <- sapply(seq_along(t1), function(c) {
  ap <- t1; ap[c] <- ap[c]+h; am <- t1; am[c] <- am[c]-h
  -(Eg(ap,t2,rho) - Eg(am,t2,rho))/(2*h) })
W <- wmat(t1,t2,rho)
alt <- sapply(seq_along(t1), function(c) sum(W[c,] * (I$u[c,] - I$u[c+1,])))

data.frame(
  check = c("E[g] at the truth (must be 0)",
            "I_rho,rho vs numeric",
            "I_rho,a vs numeric",
            "I_rho,a via the w-weighted form"),
  value = format(c(Eg(t1,t2,rho),
                   abs(I$Irr + (Eg(t1,t2,rho+h)-Eg(t1,t2,rho-h))/(2*h)),
                   max(abs(I$Ira - num_a)),
                   max(abs(alt - I$Ira))), digits = 3))
```

**Level 3 — the influence function's exact moments.** Because $\psi_\rho$ is a
cell lookup, its moments are sums over the table rather than simulations. The
naive version — the direct score with the propagation term dropped — is
carried alongside, because the size of the error is worth knowing and because
of what it reveals about the centring diagnostic.

```{r gate3-L3}
#| cache: true
P    <- cellP(t1, t2, rho)
psiG <- psi_rho_table(t1, t2, rho)
psiN <- psi_rho_table(t1, t2, rho, drop_propagation = TRUE)

data.frame(
  quantity = c("E[psi] correct", "E[psi] naive",
               "N*Var(rho-hat) correct", "N*Var(rho-hat) naive",
               "naive understates by"),
  value = c(format(sum(P*psiG), digits = 3), format(sum(P*psiN), digits = 3),
            sprintf("%.6f", sum(P*psiG^2)), sprintf("%.6f", sum(P*psiN^2)),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*(1 - sum(P*psiN^2)/sum(P*psiG^2)))))
```

Note the second row. **The naive influence function is also exactly centred**,
so the centring diagnostic of @sec-gamma cannot detect a missing propagation
term. That diagnostic catches derivative errors, not omitted terms — worth
knowing before relying on it.

**Level 4 — the decisive test.** An influence function makes a stronger claim
than a variance: $\hat\rho - \rho = N^{-1}\sum_i\psi_{\rho,i} + o_p(N^{-1/2})$.
Testing that pointwise separates the two candidates cleanly, where comparing
variances does not. If the expansion holds, the residual's standard deviation
times $\sqrt N$ shrinks with $N$; if a term is missing, it does not.

```{r gate3-L4}
#| cache: true
set.seed(99)
L <- chol(matrix(c(1,rho,rho,1),2))
run <- function(N, R) {
  dev <- Tc <- Tn <- numeric(R)
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    Z  <- matrix(rnorm(2*N), N, 2) %*% L
    Yj <- findInterval(Z[,1], t1); Yk <- findInterval(Z[,2], t2)
    ah <- qnorm(cumsum(tabulate(Yj+1, length(t1)+1)/N)[-(length(t1)+1)])
    bh <- qnorm(cumsum(tabulate(Yk+1, length(t2)+1)/N)[-(length(t2)+1)])
    n  <- table(factor(Yj,0:length(t1)), factor(Yk,0:length(t2)))
    S  <- function(rr) sum(n * dP_drho(ah,bh,rr) / cellP(ah,bh,rr))
    dev[r] <- uniroot(S, c(-0.95,0.95), tol=1e-11)$root - rho
    Tc[r] <- sum(n*psiG)/N; Tn[r] <- sum(n*psiN)/N
  }
  c(cor_correct = cor(dev,Tc), resid_correct = sd(dev-Tc)*sqrt(N),
    cor_naive   = cor(dev,Tn), resid_naive   = sd(dev-Tn)*sqrt(N))
}
out <- t(sapply(c(2000, 8000), run, R = 150))
data.frame(N = c(2000, 8000), round(out, 5))
```

`resid_correct` should roughly halve as $N$ quadruples, and `resid_naive`
should not move. That difference — a residual that vanishes at the right rate
versus one that does not vanish at all — is the whole content of the claim.

**Level 5 — reduction to the binary oracle.** The spec's stated acceptance
test: the general machinery must reproduce the independently derived closed
form of @sec-oracle when both variables are binary, across the parameter
space rather than at one point.

```{r gate3-L5}
#| cache: true
worst <- 0
for (q1 in c(.15,.30,.50,.75)) for (q2 in c(.25,.50,.60))
  for (rr in c(-.6,-.2,.3,.5,.8)) {
    A <- qnorm(q1); B <- qnorm(q2); sg <- sqrt(1-rr^2)
    p0 <- Phi2(A,B,rr); d2 <- phi2(A,B,rr)
    cf <- outer(1:2, 1:2, Vectorize(function(r,s)
          (((r==1)*(s==1) - p0) - pnorm((B-rr*A)/sg)*((r==1) - q1)
                                - pnorm((A-rr*B)/sg)*((s==1) - q2)) / d2))
    worst <- max(worst, max(abs(psi_rho_table(A, B, rr) - cf)))
  }
data.frame(combinations = 60, max_abs_difference = format(worst, digits = 3))
```

### Which information normalises $\psi_\rho$ {#sec-normaliser}

The boxed result divides by $I_{\rho\rho}$ and weights by $I_{\rho a_c}$, and both are
*expected* informations — sums over the table against the model-implied cell
probabilities $\pi_{rs}(\hat a, \hat b, \hat\rho)$. **Nothing in the derivation requires
that.** The two-step expansion asks for $A = -E[\partial g_i/\partial\rho]$ and
$G_{a_c} = E[\partial g_i/\partial a_c]$, and any consistent estimator of those
expectations yields a valid influence function. The obvious alternative weights by the
*observed* cell proportions $\hat\pi_{rs} = n_{rs}/N$, which turns both into literal
per-observation crossproducts — the outer-product, or BHHH, form.

Both are written at once by making the weight matrix an argument:

$$\hat I_{\rho\rho}(W) = \sum_{rs} W_{rs}\,u_{rs}^2,
\qquad
\hat I_{\rho a_c}(W) = \sum_{rs} W_{rs}\,u_{rs}\,
   \frac{\partial_{a_c}\pi_{rs}}{\pi_{rs}}.$$

$W = \pi$ recovers the boxed expected form. $W = \hat\pi$ gives the empirical one.

**lavaan uses $W = \hat\pi$**, and that is a fact about its code rather than an inference
from its output. `lavaan:::muthen1984()` assembles a per-observation score matrix `sc`
and returns `b_inv %*% crossprod(sc) %*% t(b_inv)`, so its $\psi_i = B^{-1}sc_i$ has
exactly the two-step shape derived above — but its blocks of $B$ are
`a22[i,i] <- sum(sc_cor[,i]^2)` and
`a21[...] <- crossprod(sc_cor[,pstar], pair$dx_th_i)`, outer products of observed
scores, not table sums against $\pi$. Read from lavaan 0.7.2 on 2026-09-20.

> The chunks in this subsection were executed under R 4.6.0 on 2026-09-20 by extracting
> them and running them in sequence against this file's earlier definitions. Quarto is
> not installed on the development machine, so the document as a whole has not been
> re-rendered and the numbers quoted in the prose below come from that run.

```{r norm-core}
infoW <- function(a, b, rho, W) {
  P <- cellP(a,b,rho); Pr <- dP_drho(a,b,rho); u <- Pr/P
  list(P = P, u = u,
       Irr = sum(W * u * u),
       Ira = sapply(seq_along(a), function(c) sum(W * u * dP_da(a,b,rho,c)/P)),
       Irb = sapply(seq_along(b), function(d) sum(W * u * dP_db(a,b,rho,d)/P)))
}
psi_tab <- function(a, b, rho, W) {
  I <- infoW(a,b,rho,W); K1 <- length(a)+1; K2 <- length(b)+1
  qa <- pnorm(a); qb <- pnorm(b)
  pa <- outer(seq_len(K1), seq_along(a), function(r,c) ((r<=c)-qa[c])/dnorm(a[c]))
  pb <- outer(seq_len(K2), seq_along(b), function(s,d) ((s<=d)-qb[d])/dnorm(b[d]))
  (I$u - outer(as.vector(pa %*% I$Ira), as.vector(pb %*% I$Irb), "+")) / I$Irr
}
```

**Level N1 — the generalisation is exact at $W = \pi$.** If it were not, everything the
rest of this section verified would have to be re-verified.

```{r norm-N1}
P <- cellP(t1,t2,rho); Pr <- dP_drho(t1,t2,rho)
Ie <- infoW(t1,t2,rho,P); Wc <- wmat(t1,t2,rho)
data.frame(
  check = c("I_rho,rho vs the boxed sum",
            "I_rho,a  vs the boxed sum",
            "I_rho,a  vs the w-weighted compact form"),
  value = format(c(
    abs(Ie$Irr - sum(Pr^2/P)),
    max(abs(Ie$Ira - sapply(seq_along(t1), function(c)
                            sum(Pr*dP_da(t1,t2,rho,c)/P)))),
    max(abs(Ie$Ira - sapply(seq_along(t1), function(c)
                            sum(Wc[c,]*(Ie$u[c,]-Ie$u[c+1,])))))), digits = 3))
```

Gaps of 0, 0 and 2.78e-17 — so the compact $w$-weighted form of the previous
subsection, and the numerical-differentiation check behind it, carry over unchanged as
the $W = \pi$ case.

**Level N2 — at $W = \hat\pi$ the table sum *is* the crossproduct.** This is the
definition being claimed, so it is asserted rather than assumed: forming the same
quantity by looking up $u_i$ and $v_i$ per observation and crossing the two $N$-vectors
must give the identical number.

```{r norm-N2}
set.seed(4321)
nrm_draw <- function(N) {
  L <- chol(matrix(c(1, rho, rho, 1), 2))
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(2 * N), N, 2) %*% L
  cbind(findInterval(Z[,1], t1), findInterval(Z[,2], t2))
}
nrm_thr <- function(y, K) qnorm(cumsum(tabulate(y + 1, K) / length(y))[-K])
nrm_fit <- function(Y, ah, bh) {
  n <- table(factor(Y[,1], 0:length(t1)), factor(Y[,2], 0:length(t2)))
  uniroot(function(r) sum(n * dP_drho(ah,bh,r) / cellP(ah,bh,r)),
          c(-.95,.95), tol = 1e-12)$root
}

N <- 4000; Y <- nrm_draw(N)
ah <- nrm_thr(Y[,1], 4); bh <- nrm_thr(Y[,2], 3); rh <- nrm_fit(Y, ah, bh)
Ph <- prop.table(table(factor(Y[,1], 0:3), factor(Y[,2], 0:2)))
Ih <- infoW(ah, bh, rh, Ph)
ui <- Ih$u[cbind(Y[,1]+1, Y[,2]+1)]
vi <- (dP_da(ah,bh,rh,1) / Ih$P)[cbind(Y[,1]+1, Y[,2]+1)]
data.frame(quantity = c("I_rho,rho", "I_rho,a_1"),
           table_weighted = c(Ih$Irr, Ih$Ira[1]),
           crossproduct   = c(sum(ui^2)/N, sum(ui*vi)/N),
           gap            = c(abs(Ih$Irr - sum(ui^2)/N),
                              abs(Ih$Ira[1] - sum(ui*vi)/N)))
```

Both gaps are exactly zero.

**Level N3 — the two normalisers differ at $O(N^{-1/2})$.** Multiplying the mean
relative gap by $\sqrt N$ should give a constant.

```{r norm-N3}
t(sapply(c(2000, 8000, 32000), function(NN) {
  g <- replicate(20, {
    Y <- nrm_draw(NN); ah <- nrm_thr(Y[,1],4); bh <- nrm_thr(Y[,2],3)
    rr <- nrm_fit(Y, ah, bh)
    Ph <- prop.table(table(factor(Y[,1],0:3), factor(Y[,2],0:2)))
    abs(infoW(ah,bh,rr,Ph)$Irr / infoW(ah,bh,rr,cellP(ah,bh,rr))$Irr - 1)
  })
  c(N = NN, mean_rel_gap = mean(g), times_sqrtN = mean(g) * sqrt(NN))
}))
```

1.196, 1.361 and 1.207 — flat, as a $N^{-1/2}$ difference must be.

**Level N4 — the decisive one: same limit, not merely a small difference.** A Monte
Carlo variance cannot settle this, for the reason recorded earlier in this file — the
two differ by about 0.2% at $n = 5000$ while the Monte Carlo standard error of
$N\cdot\text{Var}(\hat\rho)$ at $R = 200$ is near 10%. So the claim is made on the two
estimates directly. The empirical-versus-expected gap must **shrink** at $N^{-1/2}$,
because they estimate the same thing; the naive-versus-expected gap must **not**,
because it does not.

```{r norm-N4}
t(sapply(c(2000, 8000, 32000), function(NN) {
  out <- replicate(100, {
    Y <- nrm_draw(NN); ah <- nrm_thr(Y[,1],4); bh <- nrm_thr(Y[,2],3)
    rr <- nrm_fit(Y, ah, bh)
    Ph <- prop.table(table(factor(Y[,1],0:3), factor(Y[,2],0:2)))
    Pm <- cellP(ah,bh,rr); Ie <- infoW(ah,bh,rr,Pm)
    ge <- sum(Ph * psi_tab(ah,bh,rr,Pm)^2)
    c(abs(sum(Ph * psi_tab(ah,bh,rr,Ph)^2)/ge - 1),
      abs(sum(Ph * (Ie$u/Ie$Irr)^2)/ge - 1))
  })
  c(N = NN, emp_vs_exp = mean(out[1,]), times_sqrtN = mean(out[1,])*sqrt(NN),
    naive_vs_exp = mean(out[2,]))
}))
```

| $N$ | empirical vs expected | $\times\sqrt N$ | naive vs expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2,000 | 0.04045 | 1.809 | 0.08373 |
| 8,000 | 0.02052 | 1.836 | 0.08290 |
| 32,000 | 0.01028 | 1.839 | 0.08199 |

The first column halves as $N$ quadruples and the third does not move from 8.2%. That is
the whole distinction: **the choice of normaliser is a finite-sample convention between
two estimators of the same $\Gamma$, and dropping the propagation term is not.** The
8.2% also reappears here unprompted, matching the figure recorded above and in
`tests/unit/test_polychoric.do`.

**Level N5 — where the two coincide exactly.** Not everywhere the sample is large: the
normalisers are *identical*, not merely close, whenever the table is saturated, because
then $\hat\pi = \pi$ by construction.

```{r norm-N5}
set.seed(7)
Lb <- chol(matrix(c(1,.5,.5,1),2)); Zb <- matrix(rnorm(6000), 3000, 2) %*% Lb
Yb <- cbind(as.integer(Zb[,1] > qnorm(.3)), as.integer(Zb[,2] > qnorm(.45)))
ab <- nrm_thr(Yb[,1], 2); bb <- nrm_thr(Yb[,2], 2)
rb <- uniroot(function(r) {
  n <- table(factor(Yb[,1],0:1), factor(Yb[,2],0:1))
  sum(n * dP_drho(ab,bb,r) / cellP(ab,bb,r)) }, c(-.95,.95), tol = 1e-12)$root
Pb <- prop.table(table(factor(Yb[,1],0:1), factor(Yb[,2],0:1)))
data.frame(check = c("|pihat - pi|", "|Ihat_rr - I_rr|", "worst psi gap"),
           value = format(c(
             max(abs(Pb - cellP(ab,bb,rb))),
             abs(infoW(ab,bb,rb,Pb)$Irr - infoW(ab,bb,rb,cellP(ab,bb,rb))$Irr),
             max(abs(psi_tab(ab,bb,rb,Pb) - psi_tab(ab,bb,rb,cellP(ab,bb,rb))))),
             digits = 3))
```

5.55e-17, 1.11e-16 and 8.88e-16. Two consequences worth carrying forward. The
**univariate** threshold model is saturated too, so the whole threshold block of $\Gamma$
is untouched by this choice — which is why it agrees between implementations at 1e-13
while the correlation block does not. And a **binary pair** is saturated, so Cases A and
B of the spec cannot detect the difference at all: sub-phase 4a would pass clean under
either normaliser, and only $K > 2$ separates them.

### What v1 ships, and why

**v1 ships $W = \hat\pi$.** The argument is compatibility, and it is the same argument
@sec-gamma already made one level up: production builds $\hat\Gamma$ as an empirical
outer product rather than a plug-in *because lavaan does*, and an $O(N^{-1/2})$
disagreement with the primary reference gets reported as a standard-error bug rather than
as a modelling convention. That reasoning applies unchanged to the normaliser inside
$\psi$, and the size is not academic: on `case_D` at $n = 5000$ the expected form differs
from `lavInspect(fit, "gamma")` by 0.051 absolute and 6.56 relative, against 9.07e-10 and
1.17e-09 for the empirical form. Both figures were reproduced in R on 2026-09-20 and are
asserted from inside Stata in `tests/unit/test_gamma.do`.

Corroboration that this is not merely tracking one package: lavaan and Mplus agree on
`case_D`'s $z$ statistics to about 1.1e-4 relative, where the two normalisers imply
standard errors differing by 2 to 3%. Mplus is therefore on the same side, inferred
through the sandwich rather than observed directly, since Mplus does not expose $\Gamma$.

The expected form is not discarded. `dwlsmv_pairinfo()` takes the weight matrix as an
argument precisely so both remain reachable: $W = \pi$ is the unit-test oracle that Level
N1 validates, and it is the candidate fallback if the empirical form turns out to be the
worse-behaved of the two under sparse cells — where $\hat\pi$ gives an empty cell zero
weight and drops it, while $\pi$ retains it. That question is open and belongs with the
sparse-cell policy in E-001, not here. At $W = \pi$ an empty cell keeps its
model weight, so near $\rho = \pm1$, where a corner cell's computed probability is
rounding noise, the oracle is undefined rather than merely inaccurate (@sec-emptycells).

### What remains

Gate 3 is closed for the pairwise influence functions. Still open at the Γ
level: the cross-pair entries $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\rho_{jk},
\hat\rho_{lm})$. Nothing above computes them, and nothing needs to — they fall
out of the empirical outer product $N^{-1}\sum_i\hat\psi_i\hat\psi_i'$ once
every $\psi$ is correct, which is the whole reason production uses that
construction rather than assembling Γ analytically. An analytic form would
need trivariate normal probabilities when two pairs share an index and
quadrivariate when they share none.


## Gate 5: the WLSMV scaled-and-shifted statistic {#sec-gate5}

This closes Gate 5. Two source documents are needed, and the spec's v4 citation
named only the first:

- **Muthén, du Toit & Spisic (1997)** supplies the residual-weight matrix $U$
  (their eq. 14), the mean-adjusted statistic $T_1$ (12–13), and the
  Satterthwaite statistic $T_2$ (15–16). It contains **no shift parameter**.
- **Asparouhov & Muthén (2010), "Simple Second Order Chi-Square Correction"**
  supplies the scale-and-shift $T_3$ (their eq. 4), which is the v1 target.

### The three statistics

Let $T$ be the minimised fit function value scaled by the sample size,
$T = (N-1)\,F(\hat\theta)$, let $D$ be the model degrees of freedom, and let

$$M = U\Gamma, \qquad
U = W_D - W_D\Delta(\Delta' W_D \Delta)^{-1}\Delta' W_D .$$

$T$ is asymptotically distributed as $\sum_{d=1}^{D} w_d\,\chi^2_1$ with the
$w_d$ the nonzero eigenvalues of $M$, hence $E(T) = \operatorname{Tr}(M)$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(T) = 2\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)$.

**$N-1$, not $N$, is a compatibility convention and not a result.** $N F$ and
$(N-1)F$ have the same limit, so nothing in this section depends on the choice,
and the chunks below never use $N$ at all. The two reference tools differ on
it. lavaan 0.7.2 scales the DWLS objective by $\tfrac12 (N-1)/N$ in
`lav_model_objective()` and multiplies by $2N$ in `lav_model_test()`, giving
$(N-1)F$; Mplus uses $N F$. Measured on case D, first in a throwaway Stata diagnostic and since 2026-09-24 asserted by `tests/unit/test_inference.do` check 4, by computing $T_3$ both ways from
our own $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$: $(N-1)F$ reproduces lavaan's `scaled.shifted`
statistic to $2.1\times10^{-8}$ relative and $N F$ reproduces Mplus's to
$9.5\times10^{-6}$, while each misses the other tool by $\approx 1/N$. dwlsmv
follows lavaan (decided 2026-09-23; spec §4.9). Because $a$ and $b$ do not
involve $T$, the two conventions give $T_3$ values $a F(\hat\theta)$ apart --
at most $1/(N-1)$ relative, since $b \ge 0$ ($\operatorname{Tr}(M)^2 \le
D\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)$ over $D$ nonzero eigenvalues) -- which is inside spec
§7.2's $10^{-3}$ test-statistic tier as it stood until 2026-09-24. That is why no tolerance ever surfaced it (the current $10^{-5}$ tier does), and why the check that first did is
`tests/unit/test_fit.do` check 5, which requires lavaan's unscaled $\chi^2$ to
match $(N-1)F$ and **not** $N F$.

| | Statistic | df | lavaan | Mplus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $T_1$ | $T\,D/\operatorname{Tr}(M)$ | $D$ | `satorra.bentler`-style first order | WLSM |
| $T_2$ | $T\,\hat D/\operatorname{Tr}(M)$, $\hat D = \big[\operatorname{Tr}(M)^2/\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)\big]$ | $\hat D$ | `mean.var.adjusted` | WLSMV, `Satterthwaite=ON` |
| $T_3$ | $aT + b$ | $D$ | `scaled.shifted` | WLSMV (V6+ default) |

**The v1 target is $T_3$.** Table 1 of the 2010 note settles the naming:
`Satterthwaite=OFF` — the Mplus V6 default — is $T_3$, and that is what lavaan
calls `scaled.shifted`. The spec's choice of target was right all along; only
its source attribution was wrong.

### Deriving $a$ and $b$

Require $T_3 = aT+b$ to match both moments of $\chi^2_D$:

$$D = a\operatorname{Tr}(M) + b, \qquad 2D = 2a^2\operatorname{Tr}(M^2).$$

The second equation gives $a$ alone, and the first then gives $b$:

$$\boxed{\;a = \sqrt{\frac{D}{\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)}},
\qquad
b = D - \sqrt{\frac{D\,\operatorname{Tr}(M)^2}{\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)}}\;}$$

Note $T_3$ keeps $D$ degrees of freedom. That is the whole point of the
construction: $T_2$ buys its second moment by *estimating* the degrees of
freedom and rounding to an integer, while $T_3$ buys it with an additive shift
and leaves $df$ alone.

### A notational trap worth stating explicitly

**Muthén et al.'s $W$ is the inverse of this spec's $W_D$.** Their fit function
is $(s-\sigma)'W^{-1}(s-\sigma)$ and their eq. (14) reads $U = W^{-1} -
W^{-1}\Delta(\Delta'W^{-1}\Delta)^{-1}\Delta'W^{-1}$. The spec writes the fit
function as $(s-\sigma)'W_D(s-\sigma)$ with $W_D = \operatorname{diag}(\Gamma)^{-1}$,
so **their $W^{-1}$ is our $W_D$** and the formulas above are already in this
document's convention. Substituting $\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma)^{-1}$ where the
paper writes $W$ inverts the weight matrix and silently produces a completely
wrong $U$. This is exactly the kind of error that runs without complaint.

### Verification

Everything below uses **synthetic** $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$. That is not a
shortcut: $a$ and $b$ are linear algebra on $U$ and $\Gamma$, so the correction
is verifiable with any conformable pair. What this section does *not* verify is
that our $\Gamma$ is right (Gates 3 and 4), that our $\Delta$ is right (Gate 2),
or that the result agrees with lavaan's implementation — that last one is
Module 9's validation task and needs real fixtures.

```{r gate5-setup}
#| cache: true
trc  <- function(A) sum(diag(A))
Umat <- function(Gm, Dl) {                 # spec convention: W_D = diag(Gamma)^{-1}
  W <- diag(1/diag(Gm))
  W - W %*% Dl %*% solve(t(Dl) %*% W %*% Dl) %*% t(Dl) %*% W
}
corrections <- function(M, Ddf) {
  m1 <- trc(M); m2 <- trc(M %*% M)
  list(trM = m1, trM2 = m2,
       s1  = Ddf / m1,                                   # T1 scale
       Dhat = round(m1^2 / m2),
       s2  = round(m1^2 / m2) / m1,                      # T2 scale
       a   = sqrt(Ddf / m2),
       b   = Ddf - sqrt(Ddf * m1^2 / m2))
}

set.seed(11)
pstar <- 16; nfree <- 6; Ddf <- pstar - nfree   # e.g. 10 thresholds + 6 correlations
Amat  <- matrix(rnorm(pstar^2), pstar)
Gsyn  <- crossprod(Amat)/pstar + diag(pstar)
Dsyn  <- matrix(rnorm(pstar*nfree), pstar, nfree)
Msyn  <- Umat(Gsyn, Dsyn) %*% Gsyn
S     <- corrections(Msyn, Ddf)
```

**Level 1 — structure and exact moment matching.** $U$ must have rank $D$, $M$
must have $D$ nonzero eigenvalues that are real and non-negative, and the
moment equations must hold to machine precision because they are solved exactly.

```{r gate5-L1}
#| cache: true
ev  <- Re(eigen(Msyn, only.values = TRUE)$values)
ETs <- S$trM; VTs <- 2 * S$trM2
data.frame(
  check = c("rank(U) equals D", "nonzero eigenvalues of M", "min eigenvalue of M",
            "E(T3) - D", "Var(T3) - 2D"),
  value = c(qr(Umat(Gsyn, Dsyn))$rank == Ddf,
            sum(abs(ev) > 1e-9) == Ddf,
            format(min(ev), digits = 3),
            format(S$a * ETs + S$b - Ddf,  digits = 3),
            format(S$a^2 * VTs - 2 * Ddf,  digits = 3)))
```

**Level 2 — the degenerate case.** If $W_D$ were $\Gamma^{-1}$, $M$ would be
idempotent, the naive statistic would already be $\chi^2_D$, and every
correction must collapse to the identity. This is the single strongest
structural check available, because it exercises $U$, the traces, $a$, $b$ and
$\hat D$ simultaneously against a known answer.

```{r gate5-L2}
#| cache: true
Gi   <- solve(Gsyn)
Ufull <- Gi - Gi %*% Dsyn %*% solve(t(Dsyn) %*% Gi %*% Dsyn) %*% t(Dsyn) %*% Gi
Mfull <- Ufull %*% Gsyn
Sf    <- corrections(Mfull, Ddf)
evf   <- sort(Re(eigen(Mfull, only.values = TRUE)$values), decreasing = TRUE)

data.frame(
  check = c("M is idempotent", "eigenvalues are D ones and the rest zero",
            "a - 1", "b", "Dhat - D", "T1 scale - 1", "T2 scale - 1"),
  value = c(format(max(abs(Mfull %*% Mfull - Mfull)), digits = 3),
            sum(abs(evf - 1) < 1e-8) == Ddf && sum(abs(evf) < 1e-8) == pstar - Ddf,
            format(Sf$a - 1, digits = 3), format(Sf$b, digits = 3),
            Sf$Dhat - Ddf,
            format(Sf$s1 - 1, digits = 3), format(Sf$s2 - 1, digits = 3)))
```

**Levels 3 and 4 — distributional behaviour.** The moment algebra being exact
does not make $T_3$ chi-square; it makes its first two moments right. Simulating
$T$ from the true mixture shows how much that buys, and how the three statistics
separate as $W_D$ moves away from $\Gamma^{-1}$.

The design matters here, and one wrong turn is worth recording: rescaling
$\Gamma$ by a diagonal does **not** separate $W_D$ from $\Gamma^{-1}$, because
the scaling cancels out of $\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma)^{-1}$. It is correlation,
not heterogeneity of scale, that makes the correction necessary. Compound
symmetry with increasing $\rho$ is the clean way to sweep it.

```{r gate5-L34}
#| cache: true
set.seed(303); Rrep <- 100000
row1 <- function(x, df, lbl, rho)
  data.frame(rho = rho, stat = lbl, df = df, mean = mean(x), var = var(x),
             reject_pct = 100 * mean(x > qchisq(.95, df)))

out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.5, 0.85), function(rr) {
  Gm <- matrix(rr, pstar, pstar); diag(Gm) <- 1
  Mm <- Umat(Gm, Dsyn) %*% Gm; Sm <- corrections(Mm, Ddf)
  wm <- sort(Re(eigen(Mm, only.values = TRUE)$values), decreasing = TRUE)[1:Ddf]
  Tv <- as.vector(matrix(rchisq(Rrep * Ddf, 1), Rrep, Ddf) %*% wm)
  rbind(row1(Tv * Sm$s1,      Ddf,     "T1", rr),
        row1(Tv * Sm$s2,      Sm$Dhat, "T2", rr),
        row1(Sm$a * Tv + Sm$b, Ddf,    "T3", rr))
}))
out$mean <- round(out$mean, 3); out$var <- round(out$var, 2)
out$reject_pct <- round(out$reject_pct, 2)
out
```

Nominal rejection is 5%, with a Monte Carlo standard error of about 0.07% at
this replication count.

### What the sweep shows

At $\rho = 0$ the weight matrix *is* $\Gamma^{-1}$ and all three statistics
coincide exactly, as Level 2 requires. As $\rho$ rises:

**$T_1$ fails, and fails in the direction that matters.** Its variance is far
too large — 153 against a target of 20 at $\rho = 0.85$ — because it only ever
matched the mean. Rejection climbs to 16%, reproducing the inflated Type I error
the 2010 note reports for WLSM in its Table 1. This is why a first-order
correction is not an option.

**$T_2$ becomes conservative, and the reason is the rounding.** At $\rho=0.85$
its $\hat D$ rounds to 1, and $\chi^2_1$ is a poor stand-in: variance 1.53
against a target of 2, rejection 3.9%. This is the cost the 2010 note is
implicitly pointing at when it says $T_3$ "does not need to estimate the degrees
of freedom" — the estimate is not merely an extra step, it is rounded to an
integer, and the rounding is lossy exactly when the correction is working
hardest.

**$T_3$ holds up but is not exact.** It keeps $D$ degrees of freedom, matches
both moments by construction, and rejects at 5.6% rather than 5.0% under the
most extreme spread. Matching two moments is not matching a distribution. That
residual is a property of the approximation, not an implementation error, and a
test suite should not chase it.

These are deliberately extreme designs — compound symmetry at $\rho = 0.85$
across all sixteen statistics is not what a real $\Gamma$ looks like. The sweep
exists to show the mechanism and the failure modes, not to predict the size of
the correction in practice.

### The traces without $U$ {#sec-gate5-traces}

*Added 2026-09-24, before Module 9.* Forming $U$ ($p^* \times p^*$) and then
$M = U\Gamma$ costs $O(p^{*3})$. Neither is needed: both traces expand into
quantities of size $q \times q$, $q$ the number of free parameters. This is the
route lavaan 0.7.2 takes by default (`lav_test_ug_trace_stream()`, read from its
source), so it is also the one to match.

Write $w = \operatorname{diag}(W_D)$, $E = \Delta'W\Delta$ (the sandwich bread of
@sec-acov), and

$$G = \Gamma W\Delta \ (p^* \times q), \qquad
  B = \Delta'W\Gamma W\Delta = (W\Delta)'G, \qquad
  C = \Delta'W\Gamma W\Gamma W\Delta = G'WG .$$

With $P = W\Delta E^{-1}\Delta'W\Gamma$, $M = W\Gamma - P$. Taking traces and
using cyclicity:

$$\operatorname{Tr}(M) = \operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma) - \operatorname{Tr}(E^{-1}B),$$

$$\operatorname{Tr}(M^2) = \operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma W\Gamma)
  - 2\operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma P) + \operatorname{Tr}(P^2),$$

where $\operatorname{Tr}(PW\Gamma) = \operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma P)$ was used to
merge the cross terms, and

$$\operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma P) = \operatorname{Tr}(E^{-1}C), \qquad
  \operatorname{Tr}(P^2) = \operatorname{Tr}\big((E^{-1}B)^2\big), \qquad
  \operatorname{Tr}(W\Gamma W\Gamma) = w'(\Gamma\circ\Gamma)\,w,$$

the last because $W$ is diagonal and Γ symmetric. So

$$\boxed{\;\operatorname{Tr}(M) = w'\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma) - \operatorname{Tr}(E^{-1}B),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Tr}(M^2) = w'(\Gamma\circ\Gamma)w - 2\operatorname{Tr}(E^{-1}C)
  + \operatorname{Tr}\big((E^{-1}B)^2\big)\;}$$

Cost: $G$ is $O(p^{*2}q)$; $B$ and $C$ are $O(p^*q^2)$; the Hadamard term is
$O(p^{*2})$; everything else is $q \times q$. No $O(p^{*3})$ step remains. Note
$w'\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma) = p^*$ exactly, since $w = 1/\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma)$.

**Module 8 has the ingredients, not the intermediates.** $E^{-1}BE^{-1}$ *is* ACOV,
so $\operatorname{Tr}(E^{-1}B) = \operatorname{Tr}(E\cdot\operatorname{ACOV})$. But
`dwlsmv_acov()` forms $E^{-1}$ and $\Gamma W\Delta E^{-1}$, never $G$ or $B$ — this
paragraph first said otherwise, corrected 2026-09-24 — so sharing would mean
changing its arithmetic or re-expressing these traces in its intermediates, which
would be new algebra needing its own verification here. Module 9 does neither: the
duplicated work is ~1.3% of Stage 1 (spec §4.9).

**$b$ is a cancellation.** $b = D - a\operatorname{Tr}(M)$ is a difference of two
nearly equal numbers whenever the correction is small — on `case_D`, $D = 2$ and
$b \approx 0.001$. Its relative error is therefore inflated by $D/b$; the absolute
error is the meaningful one, and Module 9's test must assert $b$ absolutely.

```{r m9-traces}
trace_noU <- function(Gm, Dl) {               # the boxed expansion; W_D a vector
  w  <- 1 / diag(Gm)
  WD <- w * Dl
  Ei <- solve(crossprod(Dl, WD))
  G  <- Gm %*% WD
  B  <- crossprod(WD, G)
  C  <- crossprod(G, w * G)
  EB <- Ei %*% B
  c(trM  = sum(w * diag(Gm)) - sum(Ei * B),
    trM2 = drop(crossprod(w, (Gm * Gm) %*% w)) - 2 * sum(Ei * C) + sum(EB * t(EB)))
}
trace_U <- function(Gm, Dl) {                 # the definition, forming U and M
  M <- Umat(Gm, Dl) %*% Gm
  c(trM = trc(M), trM2 = sum(M * t(M)))
}

set.seed(2409)
big_p <- 300; big_q <- 40
Abig  <- matrix(rnorm(big_p^2), big_p)
Gbig  <- crossprod(Abig) / big_p + diag(big_p)
Dbig  <- matrix(rnorm(big_p * big_q), big_p, big_q)

relgap <- function(a, b) max(abs(a - b) / abs(b))
data.frame(
  design = c("Gate 5 synthetic (p* 16, q 6)", "larger synthetic (p* 300, q 40)"),
  trM_gap  = signif(c(relgap(trace_noU(Gsyn, Dsyn)[1], trace_U(Gsyn, Dsyn)[1]),
                      relgap(trace_noU(Gbig, Dbig)[1], trace_U(Gbig, Dbig)[1])), 3),
  trM2_gap = signif(c(relgap(trace_noU(Gsyn, Dsyn)[2], trace_U(Gsyn, Dsyn)[2]),
                      relgap(trace_noU(Gbig, Dbig)[2], trace_U(Gbig, Dbig)[2])), 3),
  trWG_minus_pstar = signif(c(sum(diag(Gsyn) / diag(Gsyn)) - pstar,
                              sum(diag(Gbig) / diag(Gbig)) - big_p), 3))
```

### Against lavaan's own objects {#sec-gate5-lavaan}

*Added 2026-09-24.* On the committed data and the exact tier-2 calls of
`fixtures/generate/20_lavaan_reference.R`, rebuild $T_3$, $a$, $b$ and both traces
from lavaan's $\Delta$, $\Gamma$ and unscaled $\chi^2$ with `trace_noU()`, and
compare with what lavaan stored in `fit@test$scaled.shifted`. That object is the
only place lavaan keeps $b$ (`shift.parameter`); `fitMeasures()` exposes only
$1/a$, as `chisq.scaling.factor`. Then the Mplus comparison of the $N$ vs $N-1$
note above, now executed rather than recalled.

```{r m9-lavaan}
#| cache: true
library(lavaan)
root  <- file.path("..", "..")
rdat  <- function(f) { d <- read.csv(file.path(root, "fixtures", "data", f))
                       d[] <- lapply(d, ordered); d }
datD  <- rdat("case_D.csv"); datE <- rdat("case_E.csv")
wlsmv <- function(model, dat, ...)
  sem(model, data = dat, ordered = names(dat), estimator = "WLSMV",
      parameterization = "delta", test = "scaled.shifted", zero.add = c(0.5, 0.0), ...)
M_COR <- "f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3\n f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6\n f1 ~~ f2"
M_STR <- "f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3\n f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6\n f2 ~ f1"
fits5 <- list(D_marker    = wlsmv("f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4", datD),
              cor_unitvar = wlsmv(M_COR, datE, std.lv = TRUE),
              str_unitvar = wlsmv(M_STR, datE, std.lv = TRUE),
              cor_marker  = wlsmv(M_COR, datE),
              str_marker  = wlsmv(M_STR, datE))

rows5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits5), function(tag) {
  f   <- fits5[[tag]]
  ss  <- f@test$scaled.shifted
  tr  <- trace_noU(lavTech(f, "gamma")[[1]], lavTech(f, "delta")[[1]])
  Dm  <- ss$df
  a   <- sqrt(Dm / tr[["trM2"]])
  b   <- Dm - a * tr[["trM"]]
  Tr  <- f@test$standard$stat
  N   <- lavInspect(f, "nobs")
  data.frame(fit = tag, df = Dm,
             trM   = signif(abs(tr[["trM"]]  / ss$trace.UGamma  - 1), 3),
             trM2  = signif(abs(tr[["trM2"]] / ss$trace.UGamma2 - 1), 3),
             a     = signif(abs(a * ss$scaling.factor - 1), 3),
             b_abs = signif(abs(b - ss$shift.parameter), 3),
             b     = signif(ss$shift.parameter, 4),
             T3    = signif(abs((a * Tr + b) / ss$stat - 1), 3))
}))
rows5

# Mplus, case D: the same a and b, applied to (N-1)F and to N F.
fD  <- fits5$D_marker; ssD <- fD@test$scaled.shifted
ND  <- lavInspect(fD, "nobs"); FD <- fD@test$standard$stat / (ND - 1)
aD  <- 1 / ssD$scaling.factor; bD <- ssD$shift.parameter
mp  <- read.csv(file.path(root, "fixtures", "expected", "mplus_case_D_test.csv"),
                colClasses = "character")
mpT <- as.numeric(mp$value[mp$label == "chisq.wlsmv"])
stopifnot(length(mpT) == 1)
c(mplus_T3 = mpT,
  rel_gap_Nm1F = abs(aD * (ND - 1) * FD + bD - mpT) / mpT,
  rel_gap_NF   = abs(aD * ND * FD + bD - mpT) / mpT,
  convention_gap_aF_rel = aD * FD / mpT)
```

**What these show.** Executed 2026-09-24 under R 4.6.0 and lavaan 0.7.2, by
extracting `gate5-setup`, `m9-traces` and `m9-lavaan` with `knitr::purl`; the
document was not re-rendered.

- The expansion agrees with the $U$-forming definition to at most 7.2e-16
  relative on both synthetic designs, and $w'\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma) - p^*$
  is exactly 0.
- Against lavaan's stored values on all five fits: both traces and $a$ to at most
  5.7e-15 relative, $T_3$ to 1.4e-14, and $b$ to 2.1e-14 **absolute**. On
  `case_D`, $b = 0.001026$, so that absolute error is ~3e-12 relative — the
  cancellation above, measured; on case E, where $b = 0.555$, it is ~4e-14.
- Mplus, case D: with lavaan's own $a$ and $b$, $T = (N-1)F$ misses Mplus's
  statistic by 1.9e-4 relative and $T = NF$ by 9.5e-6; the two conventions differ
  by $aF$, 2.0e-4 of the statistic. So Mplus scales $NF$ with, to 9.5e-6, the same
  $a$ and $b$. That residual is far above the 8-significant-digit print
  (~2e-8), so it is not rounding; that it is Mplus's own $\hat\theta$ and Γ —
  its estimates differ from lavaan's by ~1e-5 (`test_acov.do` check 6) — is an
  inference, not a measurement.

#### Check 2's rounding budget {#sec-gate5-budget}

*Added 2026-10-28, after a measured failure; every constant here was chosen after measuring it.*
`test_inference.do` check 2 compares `dwlsmv_traces` with the $U$-forming definition at a fixed
$10^{-13}$ relative. That figure was a budget with ~140× margin over the 7.2e-16 above. Under StataMP 18
at four processors, case D (marker; $p^* = 16$, $q = 14$, $D = 2$) missed it at 1.04. The run was
reproduced, and the miss was diagnosed (E-033, item 5):
- the definition moved by at most 2 ulps across counts 1–6, while the expansion's $\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)$
  moved by ~544 ulps;
- the expansion's three terms are $27.06$, $53.09$ and $26.54$, against a result of $0.514$. That is
  cancellation $\kappa_2 = (|a_2|+2|s_2|+|s_3|)/|\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)| \approx 208$, which amplifies
  `quadcross()`'s count-dependent reordering (E-034).

A fixed relative tolerance cannot see $\kappa_2$. This subsection replaces it with a per-fit budget.

**Result GB1 (one run's error, first order).** For $f\in\{\operatorname{Tr}(M),\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)\}$
computed by either route,

$$|\hat f-f|\ \le\ \beta_f=\sum_X\big\langle\,|\partial f/\partial X|,\ \delta X\big\rangle+\phi_f ,$$

with the sum taken over the computed intermediates $X$ of the route. Each $\partial f/\partial X$ is the
total derivative with everything downstream exact. $\delta X$ is the local rounding of the operation
that produces $X$:
- an inner product of $n$ terms: $\gamma_{n+1}\sum|\text{terms}|$ (Higham's dot-product bound, with one
  more product). This covers Q4's premise (@sec-mg-sensitivity-stage1) per run.
- an elementwise operation: $u|x|$.
- `cholinv()`: TS6's backward error $c_{\rm ch}u\sqrt{P_{ii}P_{jj}}$ on $P=\Delta'W\Delta$, with
  $c_{\rm ch}=6(q+1)$. **This is assumed, not established**, as in TS6.

$\phi_f$ collects the final reductions (`sum(diagonal())`, the Hadamard sum) and the combining additions.

The intermediates of each route:
- **expansion:** $w$, $W\Delta$, $P$, $G$, $B$, $C$, $E^{-1}B$, $\Gamma\circ\Gamma$;
- **definition:** $w$, $W\Delta$, $P$, $E^{-1}(W\Delta)'$, $S=W\Delta E^{-1}(W\Delta)'$, $U$, $M$.

The derivatives follow by reverse mode through each route's own assignments. For example, for
$\operatorname{Tr}(M^2)$ on the expansion: $\partial f/\partial(E^{-1}B)=2(E^{-1}B)'$,
$\partial f/\partial C=-2E^{-1}$, $\partial f/\partial E^{-1}=2(E^{-1}B)'B'-2C'$ and
$\partial f/\partial P=-E^{-1}(\partial f/\partial E^{-1})E^{-1}$. The code below states every one.

**Check 2's tolerance.** Both routes run in the same process, so

$$|\hat f_{\rm exp}-\hat f_{U}|\ \le\ (1+\rho)\,\big(\beta_f^{\rm exp}+\beta_f^{U}\big),\qquad \rho=0.01 .$$

$\rho$ is slack for the first-order remainder, TS7's working value. The bound is absolute, so it needs no
floor near zero.

**What it assumes:** $c_{\rm ch}$, and that `quadcross()` and Mata's matrix products are at least as
accurate as recursive summation in some order (Q4's premise). It is first order. A route that drops or
changes a term is a structural error of order $|f|$, which this budget does not hide (verification,
V3).

```{r m9-budget}
#| cache: true
## m9-budget (draft): check 2's gradient-form rounding budget. Needs gate5-setup and m9-traces.
## One run's error in a trace, to first order: sum over computed intermediates X of <|df/dX|, dX>, df/dX the
## total derivative with everything downstream exact, dX the local rounding of the operation producing X.
## Local roundings (one run): an inner product of n terms, gamma_(n+1) * sum|terms| (Higham; covers Q4's
## recursive-summation premise with the products' own roundings); an elementwise operation, u|x|;
## cholinv(), TS6's assumed backward error c_ch u sqrt(P_ii P_jj), c_ch = 6(q+1), counted on P.
gg_u <- 2^-53
gg_g <- function(n) n * gg_u / (1 - n * gg_u)
gg_ip <- function(n, X) gg_g(n + 1) * X                                # inner products of n terms

## Forward computations, instrumented: pert is a named list of matrices added to an intermediate on creation.
gg_fwd_noU <- function(Gm, Dl, pert = list()) {
  pp <- function(nm, X) if (is.null(pert[[nm]])) X else X + pert[[nm]]
  w  <- pp("w", 1 / diag(Gm)); WD <- pp("WD", w * Dl)
  P  <- pp("P", crossprod(Dl, WD)); Ei <- solve(P)
  G  <- pp("G", Gm %*% WD); B <- pp("B", crossprod(WD, G)); C <- pp("C", crossprod(G, w * G))
  EB <- pp("EB", Ei %*% B); GG <- pp("GG", Gm * Gm)
  c(trM = sum(w * diag(Gm)) - sum(diag(EB)),
    trM2 = drop(crossprod(w, GG %*% w)) - 2 * sum(diag(Ei %*% C)) + sum(diag(EB %*% EB)))
}
gg_fwd_U <- function(Gm, Dl, pert = list()) {
  pp <- function(nm, X) if (is.null(pert[[nm]])) X else X + pert[[nm]]
  w  <- pp("w", 1 / diag(Gm)); WD <- pp("WD", w * Dl)
  P  <- pp("P", crossprod(Dl, WD)); Ei <- solve(P)
  In <- pp("In", Ei %*% t(WD)); S <- pp("S", WD %*% In)
  U  <- pp("U", diag(w) - S); M <- pp("M", U %*% Gm)
  c(trM = sum(diag(M)), trM2 = sum(M * t(M)))
}

## Total derivatives, by hand (reverse mode), for f = Tr(M) (k = 1) and f = Tr(M^2) (k = 2).
gg_grad_noU <- function(Gm, Dl) {
  w <- 1 / diag(Gm); WD <- w * Dl; P <- crossprod(Dl, WD); Ei <- solve(P)
  G <- Gm %*% WD; B <- crossprod(WD, G); C <- crossprod(G, w * G); EB <- Ei %*% B
  out <- list()
  for (k in 1:2) {
    if (k == 1) { dEB <- -diag(ncol(Dl)); dC <- 0 * C; dGG <- 0 * Gm; dEi_extra <- 0 * P }
    else        { dEB <- 2 * t(EB);       dC <- -2 * t(Ei); dGG <- outer(w, w); dEi_extra <- -2 * t(C) }
    dB  <- crossprod(Ei, dEB)                                    # EB = Ei B
    dEi <- dEB %*% t(B) + dEi_extra                              # EB = Ei B, and -2 Tr(Ei C)
    dP  <- -crossprod(Ei, dEi %*% t(Ei))                         # Ei = P^-1
    dG  <- WD %*% dB + w * (G %*% (dC + t(dC)))                  # B = WD' G ; C = G' diag(w) G
    dWD <- Dl %*% dP + G %*% t(dB) + crossprod(Gm, dG)           # P = Dl' WD ; B ; G = Gm WD
    dw  <- rowSums(dWD * Dl) + rowSums(G * (G %*% dC))
    dw  <- dw + if (k == 1) diag(Gm) else 2 * drop((Gm * Gm) %*% w)
    out[[k]] <- list(w = dw, WD = dWD, P = dP, G = dG, B = dB, C = dC, EB = dEB, GG = dGG)
  }
  out
}
gg_grad_U <- function(Gm, Dl) {
  w <- 1 / diag(Gm); WD <- w * Dl; P <- crossprod(Dl, WD); Ei <- solve(P)
  In <- Ei %*% t(WD); S <- WD %*% In; U <- diag(w) - S; M <- U %*% Gm
  out <- list()
  for (k in 1:2) {
    dM  <- if (k == 1) diag(nrow(Dl)) else 2 * t(M)
    dU  <- dM %*% t(Gm)                                          # M = U Gm
    dS  <- -dU
    dIn <- crossprod(WD, dS)                                     # S = WD In
    dEi <- dIn %*% WD                                            # In = Ei WD'
    dP  <- -crossprod(Ei, dEi %*% t(Ei))
```
